description: The bicameral Parliament: roles of Commons, Lords and the monarch in scrutiny and law-making.
content_html:
A Bicameral Parliament

The UK Parliament is bicameral, meaning it has two chambers: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. This two-chamber design means legislation is debated and scrutinised in two places before it becomes law. Parliament meets at the Palace of Westminster in London. Its three core functions are making laws (the legislative function), scrutinising the work of the government (the accountability function) and representing citizens and debating matters of public concern.

The House of Commons

The House of Commons is the elected chamber. It has 650 Members of Parliament (MPs), each representing a constituency — a local area of the country. MPs are elected by the public using the First Past the Post system. Because the Commons is democratically elected, it is the more powerful of the two chambers. It can pass laws, approve government spending, debate policy and hold ministers to account through parliamentary questions, select committees and debates.

The Commons is chaired by the Speaker, who maintains order in debates, decides who may speak and is politically neutral — resigning from their party upon election to the post. The whips are party officials who manage MPs’ attendance and voting behaviour. Front bench MPs — ministers in government, shadow ministers in opposition — sit nearest the despatch boxes. Back bench MPs sit behind them and can scrutinise and challenge the front bench from within their own party or from opposition.

Key Fact

MPs scrutinise the government through: parliamentary questions (including Prime Minister’s Questions, held weekly when Parliament is sitting); select committees (groups of MPs who investigate specific policy areas and publish reports); and debates (formal discussions in the Chamber on legislation, government policy or matters of public concern). Select committees can call ministers and civil servants to give evidence.

The House of Lords

The House of Lords is the upper chamber. Unlike the Commons, it is not elected — its members are mostly appointed. Lords come from three groups: life peers (appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister for their lifetime); bishops (26 senior Church of England bishops, known as Lords Spiritual); and hereditary peers (a small remaining group of 92, whose title passes down through their family following the House of Lords Act 1999). The Lords scrutinise and can amend legislation passed by the Commons. They cannot permanently block Bills or legislation relating to finance (money Bills), but they can delay Bills by up to a year and return them to the Commons with proposed amendments.

The unelected nature of the Lords is the subject of ongoing debate. Supporters argue that many life peers bring independent expertise (in law, science, medicine, the arts) that improves the quality of scrutiny. Critics argue that an unelected chamber exercising legislative power is incompatible with democratic principles. Both viewpoints reflect genuine arguments in the continuing debate over Lords reform.

Black Rod is an official of the House of Lords. The most visible ceremonial role of Black Rod is during the State Opening of Parliament, when they walk to the House of Commons to summon MPs to hear the King’s Speech. By tradition, the door of the Commons is shut in Black Rod’s face — symbolising the Commons’ independence from the Crown — before being opened after three knocks.

The State Opening of Parliament is a ceremony in which the monarch delivers the King’s Speech (or Queen’s Speech), which sets out the government’s legislative programme for the coming year. The speech is written by the government, not the monarch, reflecting the convention that the monarch acts on the advice of ministers. The Speaker chairs the House of Commons, selected by MPs and expected to be politically impartial, calling MPs to speak and maintaining order.

Key Fact

The House of Commons is elected (650 MPs, one per constituency). The House of Lords is mostly appointed (life peers, bishops, some hereditary peers). The Commons is the more powerful chamber: it can pass any legislation; the Lords can delay Bills and propose amendments but cannot permanently block them. Finance Bills (relating to taxation and spending) cannot be delayed by the Lords under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949.

One viewpoint is that the Lords should be reformed to include an elected element. Supporters of this view argue that democratic legitimacy requires elected representatives at every level of the legislature; that appointed peers may not reflect the diversity of the population; and that the current system allows Prime Ministers too much patronage power in deciding who becomes a lord.

A contrasting viewpoint is that the appointed nature of the Lords is a feature rather than a flaw. Supporters argue that life peers with expertise in specific fields (such as medical science, law or education) improve the quality of legislative scrutiny. They also argue that a fully elected second chamber could rival the Commons and create constitutional deadlock, whereas the current Lords acts as a revising chamber rather than a competing power. This debate is ongoing and reflects genuine disagreement about democratic values.

The Role of the Opposition

The largest party not in government forms the opposition. Its leader becomes Leader of the Opposition and leads a ‘shadow cabinet’ — shadow ministers who scrutinise each government department. At Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs), the Leader of the Opposition questions the Prime Minister directly, putting the government’s record under public scrutiny. The formal existence of an organised opposition is a key feature of UK parliamentary democracy — it ensures the government must defend its decisions in public.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Analyse’ question about Parliament, examiners look for two-sided analysis and at least one named example from parliamentary process. A common error is writing only about the House of Commons and ignoring the Lords, or vice versa. The strongest answers weigh both chambers against the purpose of Parliament (making law, scrutinising government, representing citizens) and reach a substantiated judgement. Named examples that lift an answer into the higher bands include: select committees, PMQs, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the State Opening of Parliament and the role of the Speaker. For 12-mark ‘Evaluate,’ your conclusion must add evaluative thinking beyond summarising earlier points — “on balance, Parliament is effective at scrutiny because … however its limits are … therefore …”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Parliament is bicameral: the elected House of Commons (650 MPs) and the mostly appointed House of Lords work together to make and scrutinise laws, with the Commons being the dominant chamber.
  • Key parliamentary roles include the Speaker (chairs the Commons, politically neutral), whips (manage party voting), Black Rod (ceremonial summons), and front and back bench MPs with distinct responsibilities.
  • Parliament holds the government to account through parliamentary questions, select committees and debates; the opposition plays a formal role in scrutiny, led by the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow cabinet.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a bicameral parliament?
A) A parliament with one chamber elected by proportional representation
B) A parliament in which all members are appointed
C) A parliament made up of two chambers
D) A parliament in which the monarch holds legislative power
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) A parliament made up of two chambers.

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which MPs hold the government to account in the House of Commons.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two distinct methods. Acceptable answers include: parliamentary questions / Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs); select committees; debates; voting against government legislation; motions of no confidence. Two versions of the same point (e.g. 'asking questions' and 'PMQs') score 1 mark only. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks; 2 marks per difference. Example differences: (1) Composition — the Commons is elected (650 MPs representing constituencies); the Lords is mostly appointed (life peers, bishops, some hereditary peers). (2) Power — the Commons can pass any legislation; the Lords can delay Bills by up to a year and propose amendments but cannot permanently block Bills or Finance Bills. (3) Democratic accountability — MPs are elected and can be voted out; Lords members are not elected. (4) Presiding officer — the Commons is chaired by the Speaker; the Lords is chaired by the Lord Speaker. Evaluation is not required for a Describe question.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"An independent parliamentary research organisation published a briefing note in 2024 stating: 'Over the past decade, select committees have published more than 2,000 reports covering everything from NHS waiting times to national security. Despite this productivity, government departments accepted fewer than half of the committees' formal recommendations in full. Critics argue this undermines the committees' effectiveness; supporters counter that the reports shape public debate even when they are not formally acted upon.'"

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does the source suggest about how effectively Parliament scrutinises the government?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying a specific detail from the source (e.g. government departments accepted fewer than half of select committee recommendations in full). 1 mark for interpreting what this indicates about the limits of parliamentary scrutiny (e.g. the government is not obliged to act on committee findings, limiting their formal power). 1 mark for applying own knowledge (e.g. linking to other forms of scrutiny such as PMQs, opposition debates, or the Lords; noting that committees can still call ministers to account publicly). 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. weighing whether public pressure and reputational impact make committees effective even without formal binding power, or concluding that scrutiny is limited). Pure summary scores 1-2 marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how effectively the UK Parliament holds the government to account.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Presents two-sided analysis weighing the strength of parliamentary scrutiny mechanisms against their limitations. Names real-world examples (e.g. select committees, PMQs, Lords' ability to delay and amend Bills, Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949). Uses accurate vocabulary (bicameral, constituency, whips, opposition, front bench/back bench). Reaches a clear substantiated judgement.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, generally accurate, some development beyond listing.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content but largely one-sided or both sides present without development. Limited named reference.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic description of Parliament or scrutiny. Little or no named example. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text:
'The House of Lords should be replaced by an elected second chamber.'

Evaluate this statement. In your answer consider arguments for and against, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained two-sided evaluation naming real-world examples on each side (e.g. for reform: democratic legitimacy, patronage concerns, lack of diversity; against reform: expertise of life peers, danger of constitutional deadlock with two elected chambers, the Lords' role as a revising chamber under the Parliament Acts). Reaches a clear substantiated overall judgement with reasoning. Uses accurate vocabulary throughout.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both viewpoints addressed, at least one named example. A judgement is reached, though perhaps less nuanced.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some two-sided content. Limited development or named examples. Judgement may be weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of the Lords. Little or no real-world reference. No meaningful overall judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the name given to a parliamentary system that has two separate chambers?
Which official chairs the House of Commons debates and must remain politically impartial?
The House of Commons is the _____ chamber of Parliament, made up of 650 MPs each representing a constituency.
Party officials called _____ are responsible for ensuring MPs attend Parliament and vote in line with their party's position.
Match each parliamentary role to its description:
right: Chairs the House of Commons and maintains order in debates
Ceremonially summons MPs to the Lords for the State Opening of Parliament
Party officials who manage attendance and voting in their party

glossary_terms.definition: A parliamentary system made up of two chambers or houses; in the UK these are the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
A geographical area represented by one MP in the House of Commons; the UK is divided into 650 constituencies.
The presiding officer of the House of Commons who maintains order in debates, calls MPs to speak and is elected by MPs from among their own number.
Party officials in Parliament who are responsible for ensuring that their party's MPs attend and vote as directed.
A senior official of the House of Lords responsible for maintaining order in the Lords and for the ceremonial summons of MPs to the Lords for the State Opening of Parliament.
The largest party not forming the government, whose role is to scrutinise and challenge government policy and present itself as an alternative government.
